title: Can Ten Minutes of Reading Change a Whole Semester of Teaching? It May Have for This Teacher
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. shares an Amazon review from a colleague, Nora Ishibashi, describing how she began a dreaded first day teaching an online master's-level social work class in a state of anxiety, ordered Stuart's book These 6 Things, and had her outlook transformed after reading only six pages the night before class. He uses her account to argue that tiny interventions -- not major overhauls -- can meaningfully change a teacher's trajectory, since six pages was enough to reorient her toward why she was teaching, reset her sense of the point of education, and let her lower her own self-demands. Stuart then names the mechanism this small intervention interrupted: what he calls the "Workload-Pressure Doom Loop," a five-step cycle in which rising workload produces pressure, pressure degrades thinking and health, degraded functioning worsens workload management, and the cycle compounds. He frames Nora's experience as a genuine win-win-win -- lower pressure, likely better performance, and more enjoyment -- and closes by inviting readers to read the free excerpt themselves.
points: A single first-hand account (a colleague's Amazon review) is used as concrete evidence that six pages of grounding reading, read the night before a dreaded first class, was enough to meaningfully shift a teacher's mindset and outcome.

The five-step "Workload-Pressure Doom Loop" (workload up, pressure up, degraded thinking/health, worse workload management, still more pressure) names a specific compounding mechanism behind teacher burnout, not just a vague sense of being "busy."

The intervention that broke the loop for Nora wasn't a workload reduction but an internal reorientation -- being reminded why she was teaching and permitted to pare down her own self-demands -- suggesting perspective shifts can interrupt the loop as effectively as removing tasks.

Stuart frames the outcome as a genuine "win-win-win" (lower pressure, likely higher performance, higher enjoyment), directly countering the assumption that easing pressure on oneself comes at the cost of effectiveness.
quotes: It completely changed my perspective, re-oriented me to why I am doing what I am doing, reminded me of the point of education, helped me pare down my self-demands, and allowed me to enjoy my first class. Not bad for 6 pages.
The gist is that a small bit of reading — just six pages — significantly shifted what Nora was believing about teaching as she approached her first day.
In other words, a very small intervention — six pages of words, from one colleague to another — achieved an inner shift that disrupted the workload-pressure doom loop.

Workload goes up — There is an insurmountable number of things that we teachers feel or are told that we are responsible for doing. Pressure goes up — There is inevitably a portion of this un-complete-able responsibilities list that we feel inadequate to handle — it's outside of our competency areas.
In other words, Nora's experience of pressure in her work decreased, her performance likely increased, and her enjoyment of the whole deal increased as well. That's what we call a win-win-win.
